summary: לֹא (lo) “not” stands directly before what it negates — a verb, an adjective, an adverb or a whole predicate: הוּא לֹא אוֹכֵל בָּשָׂר, הַמַּיִם לֹא פֹּה. “There is no …” and “… doesn’t have” in the present are אֵין, the opposite of יֵשׁ: אֵין פֹּה מֶלַח, אֵין לִי זְמַן “I have no time” — never *לֹא יֵשׁ. Hebrew needs no word for “no” before a noun (אֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית “I have no car”, אֲנִי לֹא אוֹכֵל בָּשָׂר “I eat no meat”); שׁוּם adds “at all” (הוּא לֹא אוֹכֵל שׁוּם בָּשָׂר). The negative words — כְּלוּם or שׁוּם דָּבָר “nothing”, אַף אֶחָד “nobody”, אַף פַּעַם “never” — do not replace לֹא: they go with it: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם, אַף אֶחָד לֹא אוֹכֵל. Alone, as an answer, they need nothing else: — מָה אַתָּה קוֹנֶה? — כְּלוּם. “Neither … nor” has no word of its own: repeat לֹא — לֹא תֵּה וְלֹא קָפֶה. The answer “no” is the same word, לֹא; a prohibition uses אַל + future (אַל תִּקְנֶה! “don’t buy!”, S13).

blocks.caption: In a sentence each of them goes with לֹא (or אֵין).

blocks.title: Two negatives are correct
blocks.text: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם is literally “I don’t want nothing” — and that is the only correct way.

blocks.title: Never *לֹא יֵשׁ
blocks.text: The negative of יֵשׁ is a word of its own: אֵין. יֵשׁ לִי לֶחֶם → אֵין לִי לֶחֶם. It works only in the present: “there was no bread” is לֹא הָיָה לֶחֶם.

blocks.title: No word for “no …” before a noun
blocks.text: There is no special word for “no” before a noun: אֵין לִי זְמַן “I have no time”, הוּא לֹא שׁוֹתֶה יַיִן “he drinks no wine”. Add שׁוּם only to stress “at all”.

items: present “there is no / not have”? → אֵין
otherwise → לֹא right before the verb
nothing / nobody / never? → add the word, keep לֹא
blocks.caption: Choosing the negation

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Is it “there isn’t” or “not have” in the present? (אֵין)
Where does לֹא go? (right before the verb)
Is there a negative word? (keep לֹא too)

askYourself: Is it “there is no …” or “… doesn’t have …” in the present? → אֵין (never *לֹא יֵשׁ).
Is it past or future existence or having? → לֹא הָיָה / לֹא יִהְיֶה.
Otherwise: put לֹא immediately before the verb, adjective or predicate.
Is there a negative word (כְּלוּם, שׁוּם דָּבָר, אַף אֶחָד, אַף פַּעַם, שׁוּם)? → keep לֹא as well.
Is it a one-word answer? → לֹא, כְּלוּם, אַף אֶחָד, אַף פַּעַם alone.
Is it a command not to do something? → אַל + future (S13).
steps: Add the negative word, if any, and keep לֹא.

traps: *לֹא יֵשׁ is wrong — say אֵין: אֵין לִי זְמַן.
לֹא goes before the verb, not after it: הִיא לֹא אוֹכֶלֶת בָּשָׂר.
Double negation is required: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם (not *אֲנִי רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם).
אַף אֶחָד as the subject still needs לֹא: אַף אֶחָד לֹא שׁוֹתֶה.
The answer “no” and the negation “not” are the same word: לֹא, אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה.
אֵין negates only the present; for the past use לֹא הָיָה / לֹא הָיְתָה / לֹא הָיוּ.
There is no word for “neither … nor”: לֹא תֵּה וְלֹא קָפֶה.

seeAlso.note: Arabic chooses its “not” by tense and type (لَا, لَمْ, لَنْ, لَيْسَ, مَا); for “neither … nor” it repeats لَا … وَلَا, exactly like Hebrew לֹא … וְלֹא.
German splits nicht and kein (no + noun) and uses a single negation (niemand, nichts, nie); Hebrew has one לֹא and keeps it beside the negative words.
Chinese splits 不 (general, present, future) from 没 (have not, did not); compare Hebrew לֹא and אֵין.

notes.text: As in Russian, the negative words go with the negation of the verb: никто не ест ~ אַף אֶחָד לֹא אוֹכֵל, я ничего не хочу ~ אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם. нет “there isn’t / don’t have” matches אֵין.
As in Greek, double negation is required: δεν θέλω τίποτα ~ אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם, κανείς δεν τρώει ~ אַף אֶחָד לֹא אוֹכֵל.

As in Spanish, a negative word after the verb needs the negation too: no quiero nada ~ אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם. But before the verb Hebrew still needs לֹא (אַף אֶחָד לֹא אוֹכֵל), where Spanish says nadie come.
“I don’t want nothing” is wrong in standard English but the only correct Hebrew: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם. And “no” before a noun (“I have no time”) is just אֵין or לֹא: אֵין לִי זְמַן.
French ne … rien / personne / jamais also combines two negative words: je ne veux rien ~ אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם. Hebrew לֹא stands only before the verb — there is no second part like pas.
German uses one negation (niemand isst, ich will nichts) and kein before nouns; Hebrew doubles it (אַף אֶחָד לֹא אוֹכֵל) and has no kein: אֵין לִי זְמַן.
Hindi नहीं stands before the verb like לֹא (मैं मांस नहीं खाता ~ אֲנִי לֹא אוֹכֵל בָּשָׂר), and कुछ नहीं “nothing” also goes with the negation.
Persian negates with the prefix نـ on the verb (نمی‌خورم); Hebrew uses the separate word לֹא before the verb. Both need double negation: هیچ چیز نمی‌خواهم ~ אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם.
Marathi puts नाही after the verb (मी मांस खात नाही); Hebrew puts לֹא before it: אֲנִי לֹא אוֹכֵל בָּשָׂר.
Hebrew לֹא is one word for every tense, where Arabic chooses لَا, لَمْ or لَنْ; and אֵין is the negative of “there is” (Arabic لَا يُوجَدُ / لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ).

Turkish negates inside the verb (yemiyorum) and uses yok for “there isn’t”; Hebrew puts the separate word לֹא before the verb and uses אֵין (~ yok). Double negation is the same: hiçbir şey istemiyorum ~ אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם.

Japanese negates with a verb ending (食べない) and uses ない for “there isn’t”; Hebrew puts לֹא before the verb and uses אֵין. Both keep the negative word with the negation: 何も食べない ~ אֲנִי לֹא אוֹכֵל כְּלוּם.
Korean negates with 안 before the verb or -지 않다 after it, and uses 없다 for “there isn’t”; Hebrew uses לֹא before the verb and אֵין.
Finnish negates with a verb of its own that takes the person (en syö, et syö); Hebrew לֹא never changes.
Hungarian nem stands before the verb like לֹא, and negative words need it too (senki nem eszik ~ אַף אֶחָד לֹא אוֹכֵל); nincs “there isn’t” matches אֵין.
Swahili negates with prefixes on the verb (sili “I don’t eat”); Hebrew uses the word לֹא before the verb.
Luganda negates with a prefix on the verb; Hebrew uses the separate word לֹא before the verb, and אֵין for “there isn’t”.
不 stands before the verb like לֹא, and 没有 “there isn’t / don’t have” matches אֵין (没有时间 ~ אֵין לִי זְמַן). Hebrew has one לֹא for every tense — no 不 / 没 choice.
Vietnamese không stands before the verb like לֹא (tôi không ăn thịt ~ אֲנִי לֹא אוֹכֵל בָּשָׂר); “there isn’t” is không có, Hebrew אֵין.
Inuktitut negates with a suffix inside the verb (-nngit-); Hebrew uses the word לֹא before the verb, and אֵין for “there isn’t”.
